title: How To Handle A Disrespectful Class Clown
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Using a personal anecdote about a student who yelled a joke mid-lesson while reading The Adventures of Robin Hood aloud, Linsin argues that some disruptions -- particularly blatant, purposeful disrespect that gets a laugh from the class -- warrant skipping straight past the standard warning step to a stiffer consequence. His reasoning is that a mere warning for behavior this brazen risks emboldening the rest of the class to test the same boundary, so the response needs to send an unmistakable signal that the act itself, not just repetition of it, is unacceptable. He recommends building explicit discretion into a classroom management plan (his own poster carries a line noting all consequences are subject to teacher discretion) so that jumping straight to a stronger response doesn't feel arbitrary to students. In his account, he sent the student to time-out without further comment or a follow-up conversation, on the theory that saying more would only dilute the lesson of the consequence itself, and the behavior did not recur -- which he uses to argue that silence and firmness, not a warning first, was the right call.
points: Blatant, purposeful disrespect that draws class laughter can justify skipping the warning step entirely and moving straight to a stronger consequence.
Build explicit discretion into your classroom management plan up front (e.g., a stated line that consequences are subject to teacher discretion) so stronger responses don't feel arbitrary later.
After delivering a strong consequence, say nothing further -- additional comment or a follow-up talk weakens the lesson the consequence itself was meant to teach.
Letting a blatant disruption slide with only a warning risks emboldening the rest of the class to test the same line.
quotes: One day in the middle of teaching an unrelated lesson a student yelled out “Hey, when are we gonna read Peter Pan?
The entire class laughed. However, the behavior was disruptive. The student called out in class. It was also disrespectful because he was purposely interrupting.
Remember, as part of the SCM classroom management plan we recommend, you have the option of skipping the warning step and going straight to a stiffer consequence.
I like to add an asterisk at the bottom of my classroom management plan poster that says simply “All consequences are subject to the teacher’s discretion.
After the class settled down, I sent the student to time-out without a warning. I didn’t say anything to the student, which would only weaken the lesson of the consequence.
I also kept the student in time-out for a long while. If I recall, about an hour. After allowing him to return to his desk, I never mentioned it again.
